bull_bear.body:
- Indigenously developed, Government of India patented manufacturing process delivering product consistency at scale - a first-of-its-kind patent in the industry
- Government-approved R&D facility described as India's only one in the silica ramming mass industry, plus a long-standing collaboration with IIT Bombay and guidance from industry veterans such as Jan W Kjellberg, ex-president of Svenska Silica
- Entirely automated processing and VSI-based crushing technology, differentiating the product against conventional local ramming mass in an otherwise fragmented segment
- Distribution reach that broke geographical barriers in the industry - 27 Indian states and 39 countries, with export sales volumes up 26% year-over-year, cushioning against domestic demand swings
- Customised product formulations matched to customers' plant parameters, supported by technicians running on-site trials to optimise furnace performance, lining life and energy efficiency - management links this to stronger pricing power
- Raw material control: quartz stone procured from its own licensed mines, adhering to environmental and regulatory protocols, minimising supply interruptions
- Debt-free balance sheet (debt-equity ratio of 0.02x in FY26) enabling the Company to aggressively target new growth opportunities
- Demonstrated ability to absorb new capacity - the previous expansion was utilised in less than two years, with capacity utilisation of 87% in Q4 FY26
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Occupational health and safety - respirable silica dust and silicosis exposure — Flagged as the first material issue in the BRSR materiality table: exposure to respirable silica dust in manufacturing operations poses significant health risks, regulatory liabilities and reputational concerns. This is intrinsic to a silica-grinding business rather than incidental, and management's stated response is advanced dust suppression systems, enclosed operations, PPE, continuous air monitoring and periodic medical check-ups, with acknowledged short-term compliance cost.
- Raw material dependence on high-quality quartz reserves — BRSR flags that dependence on high-quality quartz exposes the Company to supply constraints, environmental risks and price volatility. The whole product depends on a single mineral input whose access is licence- and location-bound, which is why the stated mitigations are strategic sourcing near reserves, long-term contracts, supplier due diligence and responsible mining practices, and why the growth strategy pairs new plants with mine-owner partnerships.
- Supply chain concentration and external disruption — BRSR flags supplier concentration, ESG non-compliance and external disruptions as able to impact operations and brand reputation. This risk crystallised in FY26: geopolitical conflict in West Asia disrupted shipping routes and escalated freight and logistics costs, and the Company stockpiled inventory in March as a precaution and relied on long-standing supplier relationships to manage disruption in imported raw materials.
- Export exposure to geopolitical, freight and trade disruption — Roughly half the business is export-facing and it sits behind sea freight. Exports were slightly impacted by vessel disruptions towards the year end before normalising in April 2026, with customers absorbing higher freight costs; a repeat where customers do not absorb the cost, or where routes close for longer, hits volume and realisation directly. The MD&A also cites rising tariffs, protectionist measures and geoeconomic fragmentation as a persistent backdrop.
- Demand concentration on the steel and induction-furnace cycle — Silica ramming mass is a consumable refractory for induction furnaces, so volumes track secondary steel and foundry output rather than a diversified end-market. Management's own framing makes the linkage explicit - the growing adoption of electric-route steel production is what supports long-term demand growth for the industry - which means a slowdown in steel production, or a technology shift away from the induction furnace route, transmits straight through to the Company.
- Energy intensity, GHG emissions and the decarbonisation transition — BRSR flags that energy-intensive processes contribute to emissions and expose the Company to transition risks and regulatory pressures, and separately flags climate change and carbon-neutrality transition as requiring proactive climate strategies amid rising regulatory focus. The stated financial implication is negative up front - initial investment and transition cost - with benefits only over the long term.
- Refractory waste management and circular-economy compliance — BRSR flags that generation of refractory waste requires responsible disposal against an increasing focus on circular economy practices, with compliance cost named as the negative financial implication. Any breach of applicable environmental law attracts penalties and damages standing.
- Cybersecurity and data privacy — BRSR flags that increasing digitalisation exposes the Company to cyber threats, data breaches and operational disruptions, mitigated through IT security systems, access controls, regular audits and data protection frameworks. For a single-site manufacturer, an operational-technology disruption is a production risk, not only a data risk.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: RPEL manufactures silica ramming mass, a refractory material used to line induction furnaces in secondary steel plants, foundries and casting units, produced at plants in Newai/Tonk, Rajasthan using an indigenously engineered, Government of India patented process with fully automated processing and VSI-based crushing. It sells to steel manufacturers, foundries and casting units, and metal processing and recycling units, reaching 27 Indian states and 39 countries, with exports accounting for 48.59% of turnover in FY26. Customised formulations are developed to each customer's plant parameters, with technicians running on-site trials to optimise furnace performance, lining life and energy efficiency.

- Focussed capacity expansion: a 30% brownfield expansion at existing plants taking group capacity from 414K MTPA to 534K MTPA, commissioned in phases with full capacity expected operational by October 1, 2026
- Multi-location manufacturing strategy: establish facilities near key steel clusters to deepen regional presence and increase share in regional markets

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: RPEL entered FY26 with a combined installed capacity of 414,000 MTPA across its Newai, Rajasthan facilities, having raised group capacity to that level in 2025. With capacity utilisation reaching optimum levels in March 2026 (87% in the fourth quarter), and citing a positive demand outlook, sustained customer requirements and consistently high utilisation, the Board of Directors approved a capacity expansion at both manufacturing plants on April 24, 2026. The approved plan is a 30% brownfield addition of 1,20,000 MTPA taking group capacity from 4,14,000 MTPA to 5,34,000 MTPA, split as RPEL 1,44,000 to 1,80,000 MTPA (+36,000) and wholly-owned subsidiary Raghav Productivity Solutions Private Limited (RPSPL) 2,70,000 to 3,54,000 MTPA (+84,000). The capacity is expected to be commissioned in phases, with full capacity likely to be available from October 1, 2026. Beyond this brownfield step, management describes a multi-location manufacturing strategy - establishing new facilities near key steel clusters to increase regional market share, and partnering with mine owners to secure uninterrupted high-quality quartz supply - as the route to lifting domestic market share from 14% to 30% by FY30. Management notes the previous expansion was fully utilised in under two years, and that the Company has historically scaled to optimal capacity utilisation within roughly two years of commercialisation. The balance sheet is debt-free (debt-equity 0.02x), which management cites as the enabler for pursuing growth opportunities; gross fixed assets rose 11.92% during FY26, primarily due to investments in plant and machinery. No rupee capex quantum for the expansion is disclosed in the narrative, and capital commitments as at March 31, 2026 are stated as Nil.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Growing adoption of electric-route steelmaking is the structural demand driver: silica ramming mass is an essential refractory for induction furnaces, and the induction furnace route rose from ~29.3% of India's crude steel production in FY22 to ~38.2% in FY26, with IF capacity up 16% Y-o-Y to around 91 MT
- Roughly 30 kg of silica ramming mass is needed for every tonne of steel produced, tying industry volumes directly to steel output
- India's crude steel production reached 168.4 MT in FY26, up 10.5% Y-o-Y, with capacity of about 220 MT targeted to reach 300 MT by 2030 and 500 MT by 2047
- Global steel demand projected by the World Steel Association Short-Range Outlook (April 2026) to grow 0.3% to 1,772 MT in 2026 and a further 2.2% in 2027, led by India
- Infrastructure-led Indian demand: PM GatiShakti, Bharatmala, the National Infrastructure Pipeline, PLI for speciality steel, metro and railway expansion, affordable housing and a record Union Budget FY27 capex outlay of Rs 12.2 Lakh Crore
- Export demand resilience from Nepal, Saudi Arabia, Ghana, Turkey, UAE, Uganda and Kenya; India's silica ramming mass exports expected to rise over 20% by 2030
- Management links FY26 margin expansion to better realisations, improved product mix and operating leverage; per-MT KPIs continued to improve on higher realisations and optimised capacity utilisation
- Demand described as robust enough that the business was largely unaffected by short-term headwinds; exports were disrupted by the Iran conflict and vessel disruptions late in the year but normalised from April 2026, with customers willing to absorb higher freight costs
- Company scales to optimal capacity utilisation within roughly two years of commercialisation, which management cites as the basis for continuing to add capacity
- Debt-free balance sheet cited as enabling the Company to aggressively target new growth opportunities
- Precautionary inventory stockpiling in March and proactive raw material securing were used to manage Middle East supply chain disruption risk
- Industry shift towards precision, automation and stricter quality/environmental standards favours automated, higher-grade producers over conventional local ramming mass
- The Company continued to operate at healthy capacity utilization levels during the year, supported by stable demand visibility and a strong order pipeline (Directors' Report). No quantified order book is disclosed.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Raghav Productivity Enhancers Limited (formerly Raghav Ramming Mass Limited) is the world's largest manufacturer of silica ramming mass, the refractory lining consumable for induction furnaces, and commands 14% of India's domestic market.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: RPEL manufactures silica ramming mass, a refractory material used to line induction furnaces in secondary steel plants, foundries and casting units, produced at plants in Newai/Tonk, Rajasthan using an indigenously engineered, Government of India patented process with fully automated processing and VSI-based crushing. It sells to steel manufacturers, foundries and casting units, and metal processing and recycling units, reaching 27 Indian states and 39 countries, with exports accounting for 48.59% of turnover in FY26. Customised formulations are developed to each customer's plant parameters, with technicians running on-site trials to optimise furnace performance, lining life and energy efficiency.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Growing adoption of electric-route steelmaking is the structural demand driver: silica ramming mass is an essential refractory for induction furnaces, and the induction furnace route rose from ~29.3% of India's crude steel production in FY22 to ~38.2% in FY26, with IF capacity up 16% Y-o-Y to around 91 MT
- Roughly 30 kg of silica ramming mass is needed for every tonne of steel produced, tying industry volumes directly to steel output
- India's crude steel production reached 168.4 MT in FY26, up 10.5% Y-o-Y, with capacity of about 220 MT targeted to reach 300 MT by 2030 and 500 MT by 2047
- Global steel demand projected by the World Steel Association Short-Range Outlook (April 2026) to grow 0.3% to 1,772 MT in 2026 and a further 2.2% in 2027, led by India
- Infrastructure-led Indian demand: PM GatiShakti, Bharatmala, the National Infrastructure Pipeline, PLI for speciality steel, metro and railway expansion, affordable housing and a record Union Budget FY27 capex outlay of Rs 12.2 Lakh Crore
- Export demand resilience from Nepal, Saudi Arabia, Ghana, Turkey, UAE, Uganda and Kenya; India's silica ramming mass exports expected to rise over 20% by 2030
- Management links FY26 margin expansion to better realisations, improved product mix and operating leverage; per-MT KPIs continued to improve on higher realisations and optimised capacity utilisation
- Demand described as robust enough that the business was largely unaffected by short-term headwinds; exports were disrupted by the Iran conflict and vessel disruptions late in the year but normalised from April 2026, with customers willing to absorb higher freight costs
- Company scales to optimal capacity utilisation within roughly two years of commercialisation, which management cites as the basis for continuing to add capacity
- Debt-free balance sheet cited as enabling the Company to aggressively target new growth opportunities
- Precautionary inventory stockpiling in March and proactive raw material securing were used to manage Middle East supply chain disruption risk
- Industry shift towards precision, automation and stricter quality/environmental standards favours automated, higher-grade producers over conventional local ramming mass
- The Company continued to operate at healthy capacity utilization levels during the year, supported by stable demand visibility and a strong order pipeline (Directors' Report). No quantified order book is disclosed.

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Focussed capacity expansion: a 30% brownfield expansion at existing plants taking group capacity from 414K MTPA to 534K MTPA, commissioned in phases with full capacity expected operational by October 1, 2026
- Multi-location manufacturing strategy: establish facilities near key steel clusters to deepen regional presence and increase share in regional markets
- Backward linkage on raw material: partner and integrate with mine owners to ensure uninterrupted supply of high-quality quartz while optimising cost
- Scale the foundry segment by building a national distribution network and global partnerships
- Expand the customer base by deepening penetration across steel, foundry and casting industries, acquiring new customers, and exploring new export markets through strategic partnerships
- Enhance cross-selling: develop new refractory products through the R&D pipeline and cross-sell them into the existing customer base
- Enter high-value silica markets such as artificial marble and semiconductor crucibles by leveraging existing silica processing capabilities and R&D - stated to be in advanced stages of development
- Continuous product development under technical mentors to deliver better-performing product variants, improving customer value proposition and the Company's own realisations
- Portfolio diversification, product innovation, cost optimisation and supply chain resilience as the framing of the strategic blueprint
- Sustainability: now in the second year of sustainability reporting as the industry moves toward decarbonisation

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: RPEL entered FY26 with a combined installed capacity of 414,000 MTPA across its Newai, Rajasthan facilities, having raised group capacity to that level in 2025. With capacity utilisation reaching optimum levels in March 2026 (87% in the fourth quarter), and citing a positive demand outlook, sustained customer requirements and consistently high utilisation, the Board of Directors approved a capacity expansion at both manufacturing plants on April 24, 2026. The approved plan is a 30% brownfield addition of 1,20,000 MTPA taking group capacity from 4,14,000 MTPA to 5,34,000 MTPA, split as RPEL 1,44,000 to 1,80,000 MTPA (+36,000) and wholly-owned subsidiary Raghav Productivity Solutions Private Limited (RPSPL) 2,70,000 to 3,54,000 MTPA (+84,000). The capacity is expected to be commissioned in phases, with full capacity likely to be available from October 1, 2026. Beyond this brownfield step, management describes a multi-location manufacturing strategy - establishing new facilities near key steel clusters to increase regional market share, and partnering with mine owners to secure uninterrupted high-quality quartz supply - as the route to lifting domestic market share from 14% to 30% by FY30. Management notes the previous expansion was fully utilised in under two years, and that the Company has historically scaled to optimal capacity utilisation within roughly two years of commercialisation. The balance sheet is debt-free (debt-equity 0.02x), which management cites as the enabler for pursuing growth opportunities; gross fixed assets rose 11.92% during FY26, primarily due to investments in plant and machinery. No rupee capex quantum for the expansion is disclosed in the narrative, and capital commitments as at March 31, 2026 are stated as Nil.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Indigenously developed, Government of India patented manufacturing process delivering product consistency at scale - a first-of-its-kind patent in the industry
- Government-approved R&D facility described as India's only one in the silica ramming mass industry, plus a long-standing collaboration with IIT Bombay and guidance from industry veterans such as Jan W Kjellberg, ex-president of Svenska Silica
- Entirely automated processing and VSI-based crushing technology, differentiating the product against conventional local ramming mass in an otherwise fragmented segment
- Distribution reach that broke geographical barriers in the industry - 27 Indian states and 39 countries, with export sales volumes up 26% year-over-year, cushioning against domestic demand swings
- Customised product formulations matched to customers' plant parameters, supported by technicians running on-site trials to optimise furnace performance, lining life and energy efficiency - management links this to stronger pricing power
- Raw material control: quartz stone procured from its own licensed mines, adhering to environmental and regulatory protocols, minimising supply interruptions
- Debt-free balance sheet (debt-equity ratio of 0.02x in FY26) enabling the Company to aggressively target new growth opportunities
- Demonstrated ability to absorb new capacity - the previous expansion was utilised in less than two years, with capacity utilisation of 87% in Q4 FY26

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Occupational health and safety - respirable silica dust and silicosis exposure — Flagged as the first material issue in the BRSR materiality table: exposure to respirable silica dust in manufacturing operations poses significant health risks, regulatory liabilities and reputational concerns. This is intrinsic to a silica-grinding business rather than incidental, and management's stated response is advanced dust suppression systems, enclosed operations, PPE, continuous air monitoring and periodic medical check-ups, with acknowledged short-term compliance cost.
- Raw material dependence on high-quality quartz reserves — BRSR flags that dependence on high-quality quartz exposes the Company to supply constraints, environmental risks and price volatility. The whole product depends on a single mineral input whose access is licence- and location-bound, which is why the stated mitigations are strategic sourcing near reserves, long-term contracts, supplier due diligence and responsible mining practices, and why the growth strategy pairs new plants with mine-owner partnerships.
- Supply chain concentration and external disruption — BRSR flags supplier concentration, ESG non-compliance and external disruptions as able to impact operations and brand reputation. This risk crystallised in FY26: geopolitical conflict in West Asia disrupted shipping routes and escalated freight and logistics costs, and the Company stockpiled inventory in March as a precaution and relied on long-standing supplier relationships to manage disruption in imported raw materials.
- Export exposure to geopolitical, freight and trade disruption — Roughly half the business is export-facing and it sits behind sea freight. Exports were slightly impacted by vessel disruptions towards the year end before normalising in April 2026, with customers absorbing higher freight costs; a repeat where customers do not absorb the cost, or where routes close for longer, hits volume and realisation directly. The MD&A also cites rising tariffs, protectionist measures and geoeconomic fragmentation as a persistent backdrop.
- Demand concentration on the steel and induction-furnace cycle — Silica ramming mass is a consumable refractory for induction furnaces, so volumes track secondary steel and foundry output rather than a diversified end-market. Management's own framing makes the linkage explicit - the growing adoption of electric-route steel production is what supports long-term demand growth for the industry - which means a slowdown in steel production, or a technology shift away from the induction furnace route, transmits straight through to the Company.
- Energy intensity, GHG emissions and the decarbonisation transition — BRSR flags that energy-intensive processes contribute to emissions and expose the Company to transition risks and regulatory pressures, and separately flags climate change and carbon-neutrality transition as requiring proactive climate strategies amid rising regulatory focus. The stated financial implication is negative up front - initial investment and transition cost - with benefits only over the long term.
- Refractory waste management and circular-economy compliance — BRSR flags that generation of refractory waste requires responsible disposal against an increasing focus on circular economy practices, with compliance cost named as the negative financial implication. Any breach of applicable environmental law attracts penalties and damages standing.
- Cybersecurity and data privacy — BRSR flags that increasing digitalisation exposes the Company to cyber threats, data breaches and operational disruptions, mitigated through IT security systems, access controls, regular audits and data protection frameworks. For a single-site manufacturer, an operational-technology disruption is a production risk, not only a data risk.
